# @humaiz/shot-drop-opencode

OpenCode plugin. Every image pasted or dropped into chat is auto-saved as a
real file in the current project, so it gets a path any agent or vision model
can open (opencode otherwise keeps pasted images only as base64 with no path).

## Install

```jsonc
// opencode.jsonc
{ "plugin": ["@humaiz/shot-drop-opencode@1.0.0"] }
```

Then restart opencode once (local plugins and npm plugins load at startup).

Or via CLI:

```sh
opencode plugin @humaiz/shot-drop-opencode
```

## Behavior

- Saves to `<current-project>\dropped-images\YYYYMMDD_HHMMSSmmm_<part-id>_<name>.png`
  (extension derived from mime: png/jpg/webp/gif/svg).
- Already-local file paths are skipped — they need no saving.
- Creates `dropped-images\.gitignore` (`*`) on first run so images never
  pollute git. Existing `.gitignore` files are never overwritten.
- Never deletes anything. Never crashes opencode (all failures are caught and
  logged via `client.app.log`, service `shot-drop`).
- Uninstall = remove the entry from `opencode.jsonc` (+ `npm uninstall` if you
  want the cache gone).

See `shot-drop.md` for the full design doc (hooks, edge cases, verification).

# shot-drop — plugin documentation

`~/.config/opencode/plugins/shot-drop.js` · version 3 · built 2026-09-05

## What it is

A local, global **opencode plugin** (one file). Every time an image is dropped or
pasted into any opencode chat, it is decoded from the message and **saved as a real
PNG/JPG file** on disk, so any agent or subagent can later use its file path
(opencode otherwise keeps dropped images only as base64 inside `opencode.db`,
with no path exposed to the model).

- Runs **inside opencode's own process** — no watcher, no background process, no
  polling, no system registration. Close opencode → fully inert.
- Uninstall = delete the one file.
- Model- and agent-agnostic: it only writes files; consumers (main agent,
  spawned subagents, any vision model) decide what to do with the paths.

## Install / load

Portable copies (for installing on another PC) live in:
`C:\Dev\DUMP-MORE\plugins and things created\` (`shot-drop.js` + this `shot-drop.md`).

To install on another PC:
1. Copy `shot-drop.js` into `~/.config/opencode/plugins/` (create the folder if needed)
2. Restart opencode once — plugins load only at startup
3. Confirm the plugin list shows `shot-drop` (v3 id), then drop any image and
   check `<project>\dropped-images\`

Requires: Bun-based opencode (any recent version with the plugin `event` hook).
No config entry, no dependencies, no npm install.

Global plugin directory: `~/.config/opencode/plugins/` (loaded automatically at
opencode startup, before project plugins in `.opencode/plugins/`). No config
entry needed. Requires one opencode restart after install/changes.

## The hook, end to end

The plugin is a **v1-style plugin**: `export default { id: "shot-drop", server() { ... } }`.
The `id` is internal only (log service name, dedupe) — the plugin list UI and
`opencode debug info` always show local files by their `file:///` path
(verified 1.18.25), with or without an `id`. `server()`
is async and receives `{ client, project, worktree, directory }`. It logs one
startup line (`shot-drop v3 active, fallbackRoot=...`) and registers **one hook**:
the `event` hook (docs: opencode.ai/docs/plugins).

```
event({ event }) fires for every opencode event
  ├─ type "message.part.updated" or "message.part.updated.<n>" (v1.18+ appends
  │   a version suffix — exact-match on the bare type silently misses everything)
  └─ event.properties.part (SDK type FilePart):
            {
              id: string                    unique part id
              sessionID, messageID: string
              type: "file"                  ← only this type is acted on
              mime: string                  e.g. "image/png"
              filename?: string             ← OPTIONAL: present for file-drops,
                                               ABSENT for clipboard pastes
              url: string                   "data:image/png;base64,..." for pastes
              source?: FilePartSource
            }
```

### Decision pipeline (in order)

1. `event.type` not `message.part.updated` or `message.part.updated.*` → return
2. `part.type !== "file"` → return (text parts, tool outputs, reasoning — ignored;
   notably the Read tool's image outputs are `tool` parts, so they are never double-saved)
3. `part.mime` not `image/*` → return (dropped PDFs/MD/etc. are skipped)
4. `url` not matching `data:image/<mime>;base64,<data>` → return
   (URLs that are already local paths need no action; unknown schemes skipped)
5. Otherwise: decode base64 → `Buffer` → write file → log success

### Where files go

```
<worktree ?? directory>\dropped-images\
  └─ 20260905_140312_123_prt_a1b2_Screenshot.png
     └┬┘└┬┘ └┬┘└────┬─────┘└───┬───┘
      │  │  │   part.id      sanitized original
   date  hh mm ss mmm   (or "clipboard" if none)
```

- **Location**: the current project. Root resolution: `worktree` (if non-blank
  and not `/`), else `directory` (if non-blank and not `/`), else the session's
  own `directory` via `client.session.get({ sessionID })` (cached per session).
  The fallback matters: global sessions (`project_id: "global"`, e.g. projects
  that are not git repos) get `directory: "/"` + empty `worktree` at startup,
  which would otherwise save to `C:\dropped-images` (filesystem root).
- **Filename**: `YYYYMMDD_HHMMSSmmm_<part.id>_<name>.<ext>`
  - `part.id` is embedded in the name for traceability, but the timestamp prefix
    means a replayed/edited part event saves a *second* file — not an overwrite.
  - `name` = the drop's `filename` when present, else `clipboard`.
  - Extension derived from `mime` (png/jpg/webp/gif/svg), never from the
    filename (which can lie or be absent).
- **Git hygiene**: on first creation the plugin also writes
  `dropped-images\.gitignore` containing `*` so images never pollute
  `git status` or get committed by accident. Existing `.gitignore` files are
  never overwritten.
- **Deletion**: none. Ever. Files persist forever (user requirement). No timer,
  no cleanup, no background anything.

## Edge cases handled

| # | Case | Behavior |
|---|------|----------|
| 1 | Non-file parts (text, tool, reasoning) | ignored |
| 2 | Non-image files (`mime` not `image/*`) | ignored |
| 3 | URL is not a base64 data-URI (already a file / unknown scheme) | skipped, nothing to do |
| 4 | Clipboard paste (no `filename`) | saved as `..._clipboard.png` |
| 5 | Filename with invalid chars `<>:"/\|?*` or control chars | replaced with `_` |
| 6 | Filename ending in an image extension | extension stripped (re-derived from mime) |
| 7 | Very long filenames | capped at 80 chars |
| 8 | Two images in one message / same second | distinct `part.id` + ms timestamp → no collision |
| 9 | Event replayed or part edited (incl. startup replay) | new timestamp → second file saved (traceable via `part.id` in name) |
| 10 | No project context (`worktree`/`directory` missing) | skip + error log, no guess |
| 11 | Write failure (disk full, permissions, long paths) | caught; logged via `client.app.log` (service `shot-drop`); opencode never crashes |
| 12 | Two opencode instances on the same project | distinct names; worst case identical-content overwrite |
| 13 | Plugin load failure | isolated; opencode logs it and runs normally without the feature |

## Known limits

- **Windows MAX_PATH (260)**: if the project path is already deep, the full
  file path could exceed the limit → write fails (safely, with a log entry).
- **Growth**: `dropped-images\` grows unbounded by design (accepted; PNGs are ~0.1–1 MB).
- Only *images* are saved; other file types are deliberately ignored.

## Verification (2026-09-05 — v3 PASSED end-to-end)

v1/v2 post-mortem: v1 exact-matched `message.part.updated` but opencode 1.18.25
emits `message.part.updated.1` → every paste silently skipped. v2 fixed the
match but global sessions pass `directory: "/"` + empty `worktree` at startup
→ files landed in `C:\dropped-images` (filesystem root). v3 resolves the root
per-session via `client.session.get`. Confirmed in `opencode.log`
(`shot-drop v3 active, fallbackRoot=MISSING` + per-session directory) and on
disk: `commandcodesubinsalled-TEST\dropped-images\20260905_221556804_..._image.png`
(15 KB) routed to `vision-mimo-v2.5`, which read back the exact Explorer rows.

1. `bun -e "import(...)"` loads the module → exports `ShotDrop` with `event` hook ✅
2. Restart + live drop (Windows weather toast "Heavy rain soon", 2:52 PM):
   instantly saved as `dropped-images\20260905_143050810_prt_070e80bdb001ra02hPGUI85Q4X_image.png`
   (19.3 KB, original name `image.png`), inner `.gitignore` auto-created ✅
3. Clipboard-paste variant: pending first paste (design-identical code path —
   falls back to `clipboard` name)
4. Path routed to subagent `vision-qwen3.8-flash` → it read the file and
   described the image accurately (icon, badge "1", title, timestamp, colors)
   — dropped images are now routable end-to-end ✅

## Motivation / background

- opencode receives dropped images as base64 data-URIs on message parts and
  stores them in `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` (SQLite). Verified:
  194 images, 127 without any filename (clipboard pastes), 105 with a
  `filename` field (file drops). The model receives pixels only — no path,
  no name — so images were previously impossible to route to subagents.
- Drag-drop into the TUI is not supported (🚫 cursor); clipboard paste is the
  main path, which carries no name at all — hence the auto-save design.

# Ponytail — what I found (inspection of v4.9.0, 2026-09-05)

Installed as the **only** npm plugin in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`
(`"plugin": ["@dietrichgebert/ponytail@4.9.0"]`), cached at
`~/.cache/opencode/packages/@dietrichgebert/ponytail@4.9.0/`.

Author: Dietrich Gebert (MIT). "Lazy senior dev mode for AI agents. The best
code is the code you never wrote."

## Architecture (from reading the actual source, not the docs)

**Entry point**: `.opencode/plugins/ponytail.mjs` (default export). It bridges
to a CommonJS "shared instruction builder" (`hooks/ponytail-instructions.js`)
so that Claude Code, Codex, pi and OpenCode all read the *one* ruleset source.

**Three opencode hooks used:**

1. **`config`** — at startup it:
   - registers its 6 slash commands by parsing the markdown files in
     `.opencode/command/` (`ponytail`, `ponytail-review`, `ponytail-audit`,
     `ponytail-debt`, `ponytail-gain`, `ponytail-help`) via a tiny frontmatter
     parser (own module `ponytail-frontmatter.cjs` — split out because
     opencode's legacy plugin loader treats *every* function export of a
     plugin module as a plugin, and calling the parser as one crashed);
   - appends its `skills/` directory (6 Agent Skills: same names as commands)
     to `config.skills.paths`.

2. **`experimental.chat.system.transform`** — every turn, reads the active
   intensity from a state file and **appends the ponytail ruleset to the
   system prompt** (mutates `output.system`). If the mode file says `off`, it
   injects nothing. This is why ponytail "never drifts" — it is re-injected
   into the prompt every single turn, not relied upon to persist in the model.

3. **`command.execute.before`** — intercepts the `/ponytail` command and
   persists the chosen intensity (`lite|full|ultra|off`) to
   `~/.config/opencode/.ponytail-active`, which the transform reads next turn.

## Findings worth knowing

- **State is a plain flag file** (`~/.config/opencode/.ponytail-active`),
  not config: delete it to reset to default (`full`).
- **Mode switches apply from the next message**, not the current one — the
  command hook only writes the file; the system-prompt transform reads it at
  the next turn's build (acknowledged limitation in their own comments).
- **Scope**: the package is multi-tool by design — same ruleset served to
  Claude Code / Codex / pi / OpenCode via per-tool adapters (`hooks/`,
  `pi-extension/`, `.qoder/`). The opencode plugin is a thin adapter; all the
  actual behavior lives in the shared instruction builder.
- **It modifies the system prompt every turn** — so its token cost is paid on
  every request while active (currently running at `ultra` intensity in this
  environment).
- Nothing else: it does **not** hook tools, files, or messages — unlike
  shot-drop, it only ever touches prompts and the command/skill registry.
